headline: Hitomi is likely 人 (hito, “person”) plus 見 (mi, “see”): one's own reflection in someone else's eyes.

sources.quote: Likely 人(ひと) (hito, “person”) + 見(み) (mi, “see”), in reference to one's own reflection when staring into someone else's eyes. Compare Latin pūpilla, of the same derivation.

headline: Urusai is probably 心 (uru, “heart, mind”) plus 狭し (sashi, “tight; narrow”): something so overwhelming that one feels pressured.

sources.quote: Probably originally a compound of 心 (uru, “heart, mind”, vowel-shifted from regular reading ura, cognate with 裏 (ura, “the behind or inside of something”)) + 狭し (sashi, “tight; narrow”, Classical and Old Japanese, cognate and synonym of modern 狭い (semai)), from the sense that something is so overwhelming that one feels pressured to yield or submit in some way.

The earliest texts used this word to mean something more like "overwhelmed by how completely thorough something is (in a positive sense), or by how excessive and repetitive something is (in a negative sense)". Over time, the term was used less and less in a positive sense, and the focus from the late Heian period gradually became a negative sense of oppression and annoyance from something troublesome, repetitive, or overwhelming. Usage then shifted further, such that the term described not the speaker's own internal state, but rather the troublesome quality of the cause of the emotional response.
First cited to works from the early 900s.

meaning: to change, to alter, to vary
headline: Kaeru, “to change”, is from Old Japanese かふ (kapu).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese かふ (kapu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
Cognate with 替(か)える (kaeru), 代(か)える (kaeru) and 換(か)える (kaeru).

headline: Oba, an aunt, is likely 小 (o-, “small, young”) plus 母 (ha, “mother”), as 叔父 (oji) is 小 plus 父.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Attested in a text from 701. In turn, reconstructed as descending from Proto-Japonic *wonpa.
Likely a compound of 小 (o-, “small, young”) + 母 (ha, “mother”). Compare 叔父 (oji, “uncle”), also likely from 小 (o-) + 父 (chi, “father”).

headline: Chūshajō is 駐車 (chūsha, “(car) parking”) plus 場 (-jō, “place”).

sources.quote: 駐車(ちゅうしゃ) (chūsha, “(car) parking”) + 場(じょう) (-jō, “place”)

headline: Tadaima is short for 只今、帰りました (tadaima, kaerimashita), “I'm back right now”.

sources.quote: Short of 只(ただ)今(いま)、帰(かえ)りました (tadaima, kaerimashita, “I'm back right now”).

sources.quote: From the classical upper bigrade verb(バ行上二段活用) のぶ. Cognate with Japanese 伸(の)びる (nobiru).

headline: Uranau is from 裏 (ura, “back, inside”) or 心 (ura, “heart”), plus なふ (nau, verb modifier).

sources.quote: From either 裏(うら) (ura, “back, inside”) or 心(うら) (ura, “heart”, by extension, "inner feelings"), and なふ (nau, verb modifier).

meaning: to extend, to make progress, to grow
headline: This nobiru, written 伸, shares its classical verb のぶ (nobu) with 延びる (nobiru).

sources.quote: From the classical upper bigrade verb(バ行上二段活用) のぶ (nobu). Cognate with Japanese 延(の)びる (nobiru).
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 上(かみ)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 上(かみ)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

headline: Totemo is a clipping of とてもかくても (“no matter how, not at all”); the sense “very” is a later shift, first attested around 1910-1920.

sources.quote: Clipping of とてもかくても (“no matter how, not at all”), used with negative verbs. The sense "very, exceedingly" is a shift from the earlier sense of "no matter how", and was first attested around 1910-1920. Compare 全然.

headline: Kyū ni is 急 (kyū, “sudden”) plus に (ni, oblique particle).

sources.quote: From 急(きゅう) (kyū, “sudden”) + に (ni, oblique particle).

headline: Suruto is する (suru, “to do”) plus と (to): literally “when doing [whatever came before], then [whatever comes after]”.

sources.quote: From する (suru, “to do”) + と (to, “when, whenever”, temporal particle). Literally, "when doing [whatever came before], then [whatever comes after]".

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Cognate with 憎む (nikumu, “to hate”), 難い (-nikui, “difficult [to do]”, verb suffix).

headline: Daga is だ (da, “is, are”, copula) plus が (ga).

sources.quote: Phrase consisting of だ (da, “is, are”, copula) + が (ga, nominative particle, also used contrastively after verbs).
が is also used after verbs in this same way to indicate “the previous statement is the case, but...”

headline: Sono is そ, the distal demonstrative root of Old Japanese, plus の (no).

sources.quote: ⟨so₂ no₂⟩ → */sənə/ → /sono/
From Old Japanese そ, distal demonstrative root, with の (no) added to form the ordinary adnominal form 'that', as in 'that word', as opposed to the pronoun それ (sore).

headline: Ko, “child”, is cognate with 蚕 (ko, “silkworm”) and possibly 小 (ko, “little”).

sources.quote: ⟨ko₁⟩ → */kʷo/ → /ko/
From Old Japanese, attested in the Kojiki (712 CE) and the Man'yōshū (c. 759 CE), two of the oldest examples of written Japanese.
Cognate with 蚕 (ko, “silkworm”) and possibly 小 (ko, “little”, diminutive prefix).
Possibly cognate with Goguryeo 仇 (*gu), which appears in an ancient place name with an apparent meaning of child.

headline: Shitsukoi has no certain origin: the second element could be 濃い (koi, “thick”), and the first is uncertain.

sources.quote: The second element could be 濃(こ)い (koi, “thick”), and the first element remains uncertain. It could be 為付(しつ)ける (shitsukeru, “to accustom”), but is semantically problematic.

Another theory regards it as a deverbal adjective of 執(しっ)する (shissuru, “to insist”) and thinks that it was contaminated by 懐(なつ)こい (natsukoi, “easy to become acquainted with anyone”) and 熱濃(ねつこ)い (netsukoi, “enthusiastic; persistent”), but the earlier meaning of this word is "very rich and thick", so this theory is also historical semantically problematic.
Morphologically, just like 懐(なつ)く (natsuku) and 懐(なつ)こい (natsukoi), 執拗(しつこ)い (shitsukoi)
could be also derived from 為付(しつ)く (shitsuku, “to become practised”), but is still problematic on meaning.
